people.name: Gareth Mwangi
people.role: Engineer who designed a small indoor drone that changes its pulse rate like a hunting bat

people.name: Keiko Arashiro
people.role: Designer of a handheld guide for blind pedestrians with a sound emitter shaped like a bat's nose-leaf

paragraphs.text: On a warm summer evening, the small dark shapes that dart and swerve above a garden pond are doing something remarkable. Many of them are catching insects no bigger than a grain of rice, in light so poor that a human would struggle to see a hand in front of their face. For centuries, nobody could explain how they managed it. The answer, as we now know, is that most bats find their way by listening to the echoes of their own voices, a skill known as echolocation. They are not alone in this: dolphins and other toothed whales use the same principle underwater, and a handful of cave-dwelling birds rely on a simpler version.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The first serious attempt to solve the mystery took place in the 1790s, when an Italian naturalist released bats whose eyes had been covered into a darkened room crossed by fine threads. Remarkably, the animals flew between the threads without touching them. Soon afterwards, a Swiss surgeon showed that bats whose ears had been plugged with wax collided with obstacles and flew reluctantly. Hearing was clearly involved, yet the bats appeared to be silent, and many scholars found it impossible to accept that an animal could navigate by sounds that no one could detect. A rival theory, that bats possessed an extraordinarily sensitive sense of touch in their wings, became widely accepted, and the question remained essentially unanswered for well over a century. Only in the late 1930s did researchers, using a newly built microphone capable of picking up very high frequencies, demonstrate that flying bats produce a steady stream of calls pitched far above the limit of human hearing.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: How does the system actually work? A hunting bat emits short pulses of sound, usually at frequencies between about 20 and 120 kilohertz; most adults cannot hear anything above roughly 20 kilohertz. Some species call through an open mouth, while others send sound out through their nostrils, which are often surrounded by folds of skin called nose-leaves that help to direct the beam. The calls are surprisingly powerful, in some species as intense at close range as a smoke alarm. To avoid deafening itself, a bat tightens tiny muscles in its middle ear at the moment it calls and relaxes them a fraction of a second later, just in time to catch the faint returning echo. The delay between call and echo tells the animal how far away an object is, while slight differences in the timing and loudness of the echo at each ear reveal its direction.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Bats also change the way they call as a hunt unfolds. While searching, a bat may produce around ten calls a second. Once it detects an insect, the calls become shorter and more frequent, until, in the final moments before capture, they can reach about two hundred a second, a rapid sequence that researchers call the 'feeding buzz'. The choice of pitch involves a trade-off. High-frequency sound has a short wavelength and so bounces back well even from tiny prey, but it fades quickly in air. For this reason, species that hunt in open sky tend to use lower calls, which travel further, whereas those that pick small prey from leaves in cluttered forest rely on higher ones.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Not every bat echolocates. Most of the fruit bats of Africa, Asia and Australia find their food using large eyes and a keen sense of smell, and only a few of them produce simple clicks, made with the tongue rather than the voice box. Meanwhile, the insects that bats eat have not stood still. Some moths have evolved ears that are sensitive to bat calls, and when they detect an approaching hunter they fold their wings and drop, or fly in erratic loops. Certain tiger moths go further, answering with ultrasonic clicks of their own that may warn the bat of their bad taste or confuse its sonar.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Human technology has followed a similar path, though largely by independent invention: naval sonar was developed in the early twentieth century with little reference to bats. The ultrasonic sensors that warn drivers when they are reversing towards a wall work on the same basic principle. More recently, however, engineers have begun to copy specific features of bat behaviour. Gareth Mwangi, an engineer working on small indoor drones, programmed one of his aircraft to pulse slowly in open space and to increase its rate sharply as it approached an obstacle, much as a hunting bat does. In his trials, the drone used noticeably less battery power than an identical model pulsing rapidly all the time, without hitting more obstacles. In another project, Keiko Arashiro shaped the sound emitter of a handheld guide for blind pedestrians to resemble a bat's nose-leaf; in a small trial, she reported, users detected thin poles more reliably than with a conventional device.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Even so, the machines remain crude by comparison. A bat leaving a crowded cave can pick out its own echoes from the calls of thousands of neighbours, a feat that engineers cannot yet reproduce and that biologists do not fully understand. After tens of millions of years of refinement, the bat's sonar still has a great deal to teach its imitators.
paragraphs.label: G

section.text:
Seeing with Sound

A. On a warm summer evening, the small dark shapes that dart and swerve above a garden pond are doing something remarkable. Many of them are catching insects no bigger than a grain of rice, in light so poor that a human would struggle to see a hand in front of their face. For centuries, nobody could explain how they managed it. The answer, as we now know, is that most bats find their way by listening to the echoes of their own voices, a skill known as echolocation. They are not alone in this: dolphins and other toothed whales use the same principle underwater, and a handful of cave-dwelling birds rely on a simpler version.

B. The first serious attempt to solve the mystery took place in the 1790s, when an Italian naturalist released bats whose eyes had been covered into a darkened room crossed by fine threads. Remarkably, the animals flew between the threads without touching them. Soon afterwards, a Swiss surgeon showed that bats whose ears had been plugged with wax collided with obstacles and flew reluctantly. Hearing was clearly involved, yet the bats appeared to be silent, and many scholars found it impossible to accept that an animal could navigate by sounds that no one could detect. A rival theory, that bats possessed an extraordinarily sensitive sense of touch in their wings, became widely accepted, and the question remained essentially unanswered for well over a century. Only in the late 1930s did researchers, using a newly built microphone capable of picking up very high frequencies, demonstrate that flying bats produce a steady stream of calls pitched far above the limit of human hearing.

C. How does the system actually work? A hunting bat emits short pulses of sound, usually at frequencies between about 20 and 120 kilohertz; most adults cannot hear anything above roughly 20 kilohertz. Some species call through an open mouth, while others send sound out through their nostrils, which are often surrounded by folds of skin called nose-leaves that help to direct the beam. The calls are surprisingly powerful, in some species as intense at close range as a smoke alarm. To avoid deafening itself, a bat tightens tiny muscles in its middle ear at the moment it calls and relaxes them a fraction of a second later, just in time to catch the faint returning echo. The delay between call and echo tells the animal how far away an object is, while slight differences in the timing and loudness of the echo at each ear reveal its direction.

D. Bats also change the way they call as a hunt unfolds. While searching, a bat may produce around ten calls a second. Once it detects an insect, the calls become shorter and more frequent, until, in the final moments before capture, they can reach about two hundred a second, a rapid sequence that researchers call the 'feeding buzz'. The choice of pitch involves a trade-off. High-frequency sound has a short wavelength and so bounces back well even from tiny prey, but it fades quickly in air. For this reason, species that hunt in open sky tend to use lower calls, which travel further, whereas those that pick small prey from leaves in cluttered forest rely on higher ones.

E. Not every bat echolocates. Most of the fruit bats of Africa, Asia and Australia find their food using large eyes and a keen sense of smell, and only a few of them produce simple clicks, made with the tongue rather than the voice box. Meanwhile, the insects that bats eat have not stood still. Some moths have evolved ears that are sensitive to bat calls, and when they detect an approaching hunter they fold their wings and drop, or fly in erratic loops. Certain tiger moths go further, answering with ultrasonic clicks of their own that may warn the bat of their bad taste or confuse its sonar.

F. Human technology has followed a similar path, though largely by independent invention: naval sonar was developed in the early twentieth century with little reference to bats. The ultrasonic sensors that warn drivers when they are reversing towards a wall work on the same basic principle. More recently, however, engineers have begun to copy specific features of bat behaviour. Gareth Mwangi, an engineer working on small indoor drones, programmed one of his aircraft to pulse slowly in open space and to increase its rate sharply as it approached an obstacle, much as a hunting bat does. In his trials, the drone used noticeably less battery power than an identical model pulsing rapidly all the time, without hitting more obstacles. In another project, Keiko Arashiro shaped the sound emitter of a handheld guide for blind pedestrians to resemble a bat's nose-leaf; in a small trial, she reported, users detected thin poles more reliably than with a conventional device.

G. Even so, the machines remain crude by comparison. A bat leaving a crowded cave can pick out its own echoes from the calls of thousands of neighbours, a feat that engineers cannot yet reproduce and that biologists do not fully understand. After tens of millions of years of refinement, the bat's sonar still has a great deal to teach its imitators.
